name: Chapter 4: Moving Charges and Magnetism
description: Lorentz force, motion in B, Biot–Savart law, circular loop, Ampere’s law, solenoid, parallel currents, torque on a loop, galvanometer

cards.term: Who discovered that a current deflects a compass needle? When?
cards.definition: Hans Christian Oersted (Danish), 1820, during a lecture demonstration

cards.term: How does a compass needle align near a long straight current?
cards.definition: Tangent to circles centred on the wire, in a plane perpendicular to it; reversing the current reverses the needle

cards.term: How do iron filings arrange around a straight current-carrying wire?
cards.definition: In concentric circles centred on the wire

cards.term: Oersted’s conclusion?
cards.definition: Moving charges (currents) produce a magnetic field in the surrounding space

cards.term: Who unified electricity and magnetism, and when? What did he realise?
cards.definition: James Maxwell, 1864; light is an electromagnetic wave

cards.term: Who discovered and who produced radio waves?
cards.definition: Discovered by Hertz; produced by J. C. Bose and G. Marconi

cards.term: Convention: dot ⊙ and cross ⊗ for a field or current?
cards.definition: ⊙ = out of the page (arrow tip towards you); ⊗ = into the page (feathered tail going away)

cards.term: Properties the magnetic field shares with the electric field?
cards.definition: Defined at every point (vector field), can vary with time, obeys superposition

cards.term: Lorentz force on a charge q?
cards.definition: \( \vec F = q\left[\vec E + \vec v\times\vec B\right] \)

cards.term: Three features of the magnetic force q(v × B)?
cards.definition: (1) Opposite for − charges (2) perpendicular to v and B, zero if v ∥ B (3) zero for a charge at rest

cards.term: Define 1 tesla.
cards.definition: Field in which a charge of 1 C moving at 1 m/s perpendicular to B feels 1 N: 1 T = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹

cards.term: Gauss in tesla? Earth’s field?
cards.definition: 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T; Earth ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ T (≈ 0.4 G)

cards.term: Dimensions of B?
cards.definition: [M T⁻² A⁻¹]

cards.term: Force on a straight current-carrying rod in a uniform B?
cards.definition: \( \vec F = I\,\vec l\times\vec B \), with \( \vec l \) along the current (current itself is not a vector)

cards.term: In F = Il × B, whose field is B?
cards.definition: The external field — not the field of the rod itself

cards.term: Force on a wire of arbitrary shape?
cards.definition: Sum over elements: \( \vec F = \sum I\,d\vec l_j\times\vec B \) (an integral)

cards.term: Teacher addition: force on a closed loop or a bent wire in a uniform B?
cards.definition: Closed loop: zero. Bent wire from P to Q: same as a straight wire PQ carrying I

cards.term: Example 4.1: 200 g, 1.5 m wire with 2 A suspended by a horizontal B. B?
cards.definition: mg = IlB → B = 0.2 × 9.8/(2 × 1.5) = 0.65 T

cards.term: Example 4.2: B along +y, particle moves along +x. Force on an electron? On a proton?
cards.definition: v × B is along +z: proton +z, electron −z

cards.term: Exercise 4.5: 8 A wire at 30° to B = 0.15 T. Force per unit length?
cards.definition: IB sin 30° = 0.6 N/m

cards.term: Exercise 4.6: 3.0 cm wire with 10 A inside a solenoid, perpendicular to its axis, B = 0.27 T. Force?
cards.definition: IlB = 10 × 0.03 × 0.27 = 8.1 × 10⁻² N

cards.term: Mnemonic: direction of force on a current (or + charge) in B?
cards.definition: Right-hand rule: fingers along v (or I), curl towards B; thumb gives F. For an electron, reverse it. (Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the same: Field, Current, Motion)

cards.term: Does a magnetic force change a particle’s speed or kinetic energy? Why?
cards.definition: No: F ⊥ v, so it does no work; only the direction changes

cards.term: Charge moving perpendicular to a uniform B: path and radius?
cards.definition: Circle in the plane ⊥ B; \( r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{p}{qB} \)

cards.term: Angular frequency and period of circular motion in B?
cards.definition: \( \omega = \dfrac{qB}{m},\ T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB} \) — independent of speed and radius

cards.term: Velocity at an angle to B: path? Pitch?
cards.definition: Helix with axis along B; pitch \( p = v_\parallel T = \dfrac{2\pi m v_\parallel}{qB} \); radius uses v⊥

cards.term: Define cyclotron frequency.
cards.definition: \( \nu_c = \dfrac{qB}{2\pi m} \): frequency of circular motion in B, independent of energy

cards.term: Note: NCERT’s introduction and summary mention the cyclotron. Is its section in the book?
cards.definition: No: it was removed in the rationalised syllabus. Just know it uses ν_c being independent of speed to accelerate particles

cards.term: Electron circling in a magnetic field (Example 4.3)
cards.definition: r = 28 cm, ν = 17 MHz, E ≈ 2.5 keV

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 4.3 · electron in B

Find the missing step.

Electron (9 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at 3 × 10⁷ m/s perpendicular to B = 6 × 10⁻⁴ T. Radius, frequency, energy?
  1. r = mv/qB = 9 × 10⁻³¹ × 3 × 10⁷ / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 6 × 10⁻⁴) = 28 cm
  2. ?
  3. E = ½mv² = ½ × 9 × 10⁻³¹ × 9 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ J
  4. = 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ eV = 2.5 keV
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 4.3 · electron in B

Find the missing step.

Electron (9 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at 3 × 10⁷ m/s perpendicular to B = 6 × 10⁻⁴ T. Radius, frequency, energy?
  1. r = mv/qB = 9 × 10⁻³¹ × 3 × 10⁷ / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 6 × 10⁻⁴) = 28 cm
  2. ν = v/2πr = 17 MHz
  3. E = ½mv² = ½ × 9 × 10⁻³¹ × 9 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ J
  4. = 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ eV = 2.5 keV

cards.term: Exercise 4.11: electron at 4.8 × 10⁶ m/s normal to B = 6.5 G. Why a circle? Radius?
cards.definition: F ⊥ v provides centripetal force; r = mv/eB ≈ 4.2 cm

cards.term: Correction: NCERT Exercise 4.11 gives e = 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Right value, and does it matter?
cards.definition: e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (typo). With 1.6, r = 4.2 cm (the answer key value); with 1.5 you would get 4.5 cm

cards.term: Exercise 4.12: frequency of that electron? Depends on speed?
cards.definition: ν = eB/2πm ≈ 18 MHz; independent of speed (r grows with v, time per turn stays the same)

cards.term: Teacher addition: an electron and a proton enter the same B with equal momenta. Compare radii.
cards.definition: Equal (r = p/qB, same |q|). With equal kinetic energy, r ∝ √m, so the proton’s circle is larger

cards.term: Sources of all known magnetic fields?
cards.definition: Currents / moving charges and intrinsic magnetic moments of particles

cards.term: State the Biot–Savart law.
cards.definition: \( d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,d\vec l\times\vec r}{r^3} \); magnitude \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2} \)

cards.term: Value of μ₀/4π? Name of μ₀?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} = 10^{-7} \) T m/A; μ₀ = permeability of free space

cards.term: Update: NCERT says μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ exactly. Still exact?
cards.definition: Not since 2019: fixing e made μ₀ a measured constant, 1.25663706… × 10⁻⁶ T m/A — equal to 4π × 10⁻⁷ to 10 digits, so use it freely

cards.term: Biot–Savart vs Coulomb: similarities?
cards.definition: Both inverse-square and long range both obey superposition both linear in their source

cards.term: Biot–Savart vs Coulomb: differences?
cards.definition: Source: vector I dl vs scalar q. Direction: B ⊥ plane of dl and r vs E along r. B has a sin θ dependence

cards.term: Magnetic field of a current element at a point along its own line?
cards.definition: Zero (θ = 0, sin θ = 0)

cards.term: Relation between ε₀, μ₀ and c?
cards.definition: \( c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} \) — fixing one of μ₀, ε₀ fixes the other

cards.term: Example 4.4: element Δl = 1 cm along x at the origin, I = 10 A. B at 0.5 m on the y-axis?
cards.definition: dB = 10⁻⁷ × 10 × 10⁻² / 0.25 = 4 × 10⁻⁸ T, along +z (î × ĵ = k̂)

cards.term: Field on the axis of a circular loop (radius R) at distance x?
cards.definition: \( B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(x^2 + R^2)^{3/2}} \), along the axis

cards.term: Why does only the axial component survive for a circular loop?
cards.definition: The perpendicular components dB⊥ of diametrically opposite elements cancel

cards.term: Field at the centre of a circular loop? N turns?
cards.definition: \( B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \); with N turns \( \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2R} \)

cards.term: Right-hand thumb rule for a loop?
cards.definition: Curl the fingers along the current; the thumb gives B (and the loop’s N face)

cards.term: Two right-hand rules: how do fingers and thumb swap roles?
cards.definition: Straight wire: thumb = current, fingers = B. Loop: fingers = current, thumb = B

cards.term: Example 4.5: 12 A wire bent into a semicircle (R = 2 cm) with straight leads. B at the centre?
cards.definition: Straight parts: 0 (dl ∥ r). Semicircle: half a loop, \( \mu_0 I/4R \) = 1.9 × 10⁻⁴ T into the page; bent the other way, same size, opposite direction

cards.term: Example 4.6: 100 turns, R = 10 cm, I = 1 A. B at the centre?
cards.definition: \( \mu_0NI/2R \) = 6.28 × 10⁻⁴ T

cards.term: Exercise 4.1: 100 turns, R = 8.0 cm, 0.40 A. B at the centre?
cards.definition: 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ T

cards.term: Teacher addition: field at the centre of an arc subtending angle φ (radians)?
cards.definition: \( B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I\varphi}{4\pi R} \) (φ = 2π gives the loop, φ = π the semicircle)

cards.term: State Ampere’s circuital law.
cards.definition: \( \oint \vec B\cdot d\vec l = \mu_0 I \), I = net current through the surface bounded by the loop

cards.term: Sign convention in Ampere’s law?
cards.definition: Right-hand rule: curl the fingers along the direction of traversal; the thumb gives the positive current direction

cards.term: Simplified form for symmetric cases?
cards.definition: \( BL = \mu_0 I_e \) where B is tangential and constant over length L of the loop (elsewhere B ⊥ loop or zero)

cards.term: Field of a long straight wire from Ampere’s law?
cards.definition: \( B\cdot2\pi r = \mu_0 I \Rightarrow B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \), tangential circles

cards.term: Four lessons from B = μ₀I/2πr?
cards.definition: (1) Cylindrical symmetry (2) field lines are closed circles (3) finite at finite r even for an infinite wire (4) direction by the right-hand grip rule

cards.term: Ampere’s law is to Biot–Savart as ___ is to ___?
cards.definition: Gauss’s law to Coulomb’s law: same content, handy under symmetry

cards.term: Can Ampere’s law give B at the centre of a circular loop?
cards.definition: No: no suitable symmetric loop; use Biot–Savart

cards.term: Ampere’s law as given here holds for what kind of currents?
cards.definition: Steady currents only

cards.term: Example 4.7: thick wire (radius a, uniform current I). B inside and outside?
cards.definition:
Outside: \( \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r} \) (∝ 1/r).
Inside: \( \dfrac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^2} \) (∝ r, enclosed current Ir²/a²)

cards.term: Sketch B versus r for a thick wire with uniform current.
cards.definition: Rises linearly from 0 at the centre to a maximum at r = a, then falls as 1/r

cards.term: Exercise 4.2: 35 A wire. B at 20 cm?
cards.definition: 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ T

cards.term: Exercise 4.3: 50 A flowing north to south in a horizontal wire. B at 2.5 m east of it?
cards.definition: 4 × 10⁻⁶ T, vertically upward

cards.term: Exercise 4.4: overhead line, 90 A east to west. B 1.5 m below it?
cards.definition: 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ T, towards the south

cards.term: What is a long solenoid? Why enamelled wire?
cards.definition: A tightly wound helix whose length ≫ radius; enamel insulates neighbouring turns

cards.term: Field pattern of a finite solenoid?
cards.definition: Inside: strong, uniform, along the axis outside: weak fields between neighbouring turns cancel

cards.term: Field inside a long solenoid? Derive with Ampere’s law.
cards.definition: Rectangular loop abcd: only side ab (length h) inside contributes; Bh = μ₀(nh)I → \( B = \mu_0 n I \)

cards.term: How can the field of a solenoid be made much larger?
cards.definition: Insert a soft iron core

cards.term: Teacher addition: field at the end of a long solenoid?
cards.definition: \( \tfrac12\mu_0 nI \) — half the value at the centre

cards.term: Example 4.8: 0.5 m solenoid, 500 turns, 5 A. B inside?
cards.definition: n = 1000/m; B = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10³ × 5 = 6.28 × 10⁻³ T

cards.term: Correction: NCERT Example 4.8 cites “Eq. (4.20)” for the long-solenoid field. Right equation?
cards.definition: Eq. (4.16), B = μ₀nI; Eq. (4.20) is the torque on a loop

cards.term: Exercise 4.8: 80 cm long, 5 layers of 400 turns, 8.0 A. B near the centre?
cards.definition: n = 2000/0.8 = 2500 m⁻¹ → B = 2.5 × 10⁻² T (diameter doesn’t matter)

cards.term: Force per unit length between two long parallel currents?
cards.definition: \( f = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_a I_b}{2\pi d} \)

cards.term: Parallel vs antiparallel currents?
cards.definition: Parallel attract, antiparallel repel — the opposite of the charge rule (like charges repel)

cards.term: Do forces between parallel steady currents obey Newton’s third law?
cards.definition: Yes: F_ba = −F_ab. (For time-varying fields, only if field momentum is included)

cards.term: NCERT’s definition of the ampere (1946)?
cards.definition: Current in two infinitely long parallel thin wires 1 m apart in vacuum giving a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre

cards.term: Update: is the ampere still defined by parallel wires?
cards.definition: No: since 2019 it is defined by fixing e = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (1 A = 1 C/s with e exact); the wire result still holds

cards.term: Instrument used to measure the force between currents?
cards.definition: A current balance

cards.term: Example 4.9: 1 A on a table, Earth’s horizontal field 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ T (S → N). Force per metre for current E → W? S → N?
cards.definition: E → W: 3 × 10⁻⁵ N/m, downward. S → N: 0 (parallel to B)

cards.term: Exercise 4.7: 8.0 A and 5.0 A in the same direction, 4.0 cm apart. Force on 10 cm of A?
cards.definition: 2 × 10⁻⁵ N, attractive

cards.term: Intuition: why do parallel currents attract?
cards.definition: Between the wires their circular fields oppose (weak); outside they add (strong). Wires get pushed towards the weak-field region — towards each other

cards.term: Rectangular loop in a uniform B: net force? Torque?
cards.definition: Net force 0; torque \( \tau = IAB\sin\theta \) (θ between normal and B)

cards.term: Why does the torque on a loop fall as it turns towards θ = 0?
cards.definition: The forces on AB and CD stay IbB but the perpendicular distance between them (a sin θ) shrinks

cards.term: Magnetic moment of a current loop? Unit and dimensions?
cards.definition: \( \vec m = NI\vec A \) (direction by right-hand thumb rule); A m² (= J/T), [L²A]

cards.term: Torque on a magnetic dipole in B (vector)?
cards.definition: \( \vec\tau = \vec m\times\vec B \) — analogue of τ = p × E

cards.term: Stable and unstable equilibrium of a loop in B?
cards.definition: Stable: m parallel to B. Unstable: m antiparallel

cards.term: Teacher addition: potential energy of a magnetic dipole in B?
cards.definition: \( U = -\vec m\cdot\vec B = -mB\cos\theta \)

cards.term: Coil rotating in a magnetic field (Example 4.10)
cards.definition: m ≈ 10 A m²; τ from 0 to 20 N m; ½𝐼ω² = mB → ω = 20 s⁻¹

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 4.10 · coil released in B

Find the missing step.

100 turns, R = 10 cm, 3.2 A; B = 2 T with the axis initially along B; the coil turns 90°. Torques, and angular speed (moment of inertia 0.1 kg m²)?
  1. m = NIπR² = 100 × 3.2 × 3.14 × 10⁻² ≈ 10 A m²
  2. τ = mB sin θ: 0 at the start, 20 N m at 90°
  3. ?
  4. ω = √(2 × 20/0.1) = 20 rad/s
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 4.10 · coil released in B

Find the missing step.

100 turns, R = 10 cm, 3.2 A; B = 2 T with the axis initially along B; the coil turns 90°. Torques, and angular speed (moment of inertia 0.1 kg m²)?
  1. m = NIπR² = 100 × 3.2 × 3.14 × 10⁻² ≈ 10 A m²
  2. τ = mB sin θ: 0 at the start, 20 N m at 90°
  3. Work done by field over 90° = mB(1 − cos 90°) = 20 J = ½ 𝐼ω²
  4. ω = √(2 × 20/0.1) = 20 rad/s

cards.term: Correction: in Example 4.10, “initially the axis of the coil is along the field” and the coil then rotates 90°. Would it rotate on its own?
cards.definition: No: θ = 0 is stable equilibrium (zero torque); the example only works if it starts at 90° and swings to 0°. The numbers (τ 0 ↔ 20 N m, ω = 20 s⁻¹) are unaffected

cards.term: Example 4.11(a): can a uniform B spin a horizontal loop about the vertical axis?
cards.definition: No: τ = IA × B is always in the plane of the loop, never vertical

cards.term: Example 4.11(b): stable orientation of a loop in B? What about the flux?
cards.definition: Area vector along B; then the loop’s own field adds to B, giving maximum total flux

cards.term: Example 4.11(c): why does a flexible irregular current loop become circular?
cards.definition: To maximise flux: a circle encloses the most area for a given perimeter

cards.term: Exercise 4.9: square coil, side 10 cm, 20 turns, 12 A; normal at 30° to B = 0.80 T. Torque?
cards.definition: NIAB sin 30° = 0.96 N m

cards.term: Exercise 4.13: 30 turns, R = 8.0 cm, 6.0 A, B = 1.0 T at 60° to the normal. Counter-torque? Irregular coil of equal area?
cards.definition: 3.1 N m; unchanged — torque depends only on area, not shape

cards.term: Field of a current loop far away on its axis?
cards.definition: \( B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{x^3} \) — like the axial field of an electric dipole

cards.term: Field of a loop far away in its own plane?
cards.definition: \( B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{x^3} \) (equatorial field)

cards.term: Substitutions that turn electric dipole formulas into magnetic ones?
cards.definition: \( p \to m,\ E \to B,\ \dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_0} \to \mu_0 \)

cards.term: Fundamental difference between electric and magnetic dipoles?
cards.definition: An electric dipole is made of two charges; magnetic monopoles are not known — the current loop is the most elementary magnetic element

cards.term: Ampere’s hypothesis? Is it the whole story?
cards.definition: All magnetism comes from circulating currents. Partly true: electrons and protons also have intrinsic magnetic moments

cards.term: Principle of a moving coil galvanometer?
cards.definition: Torque NIAB on a coil in a radial field is balanced by the spring’s restoring torque kφ

cards.term: Why is the field in a galvanometer radial? Role of the soft-iron core?
cards.definition: Radial field keeps the coil’s plane along B, so sin θ = 1 at every deflection (linear scale); the core makes it radial and stronger

cards.term: Deflection of a galvanometer?
cards.definition: \( \varphi = \left(\dfrac{NAB}{k}\right) I \) (k = torsional constant, restoring torque per unit twist)

cards.term: Current sensitivity? Voltage sensitivity?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{\varphi}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{k},\quad \dfrac{\varphi}{V} = \dfrac{NAB}{kR} \)

cards.term: Doubling the turns: effect on current and voltage sensitivity?
cards.definition: Current sensitivity doubles; resistance also doubles, so voltage sensitivity is unchanged

cards.term: Why can’t a galvanometer be used directly as an ammeter?
cards.definition: It is very sensitive (full-scale ~μA) and has a large resistance that would change the circuit current

cards.term: How is a galvanometer converted to an ammeter?
cards.definition: A small shunt r_s in parallel; net resistance ≈ r_s

cards.term: How is a galvanometer converted to a voltmeter?
cards.definition: A large resistance R in series; net resistance ≈ R, so it draws little current

cards.term: Teacher addition: shunt needed for full-scale current I (galvanometer G, full scale I_g)? Series R for voltage V?
cards.definition: \( S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g},\quad R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G \)

cards.term: Ideal ammeter and ideal voltmeter resistances?
cards.definition: Ammeter: zero; voltmeter: infinite

cards.term: Galvanometer used as a null detector (bridge): pointer zero where?
cards.definition: In the middle of the scale, deflecting left or right with current direction

cards.term:
Example 4.12: 3 V across 3 Ω. Current read by
(a) a 60 Ω galvanometer
(b) with a 0.02 Ω shunt
(c) an ideal ammeter?
cards.definition: (a) 3/63 = 0.048 A (b) 3/3.02 = 0.99 A (c) 1.00 A

cards.term: Exercise 4.10: M1 (10 Ω, 30 turns, 3.6 × 10⁻³ m², 0.25 T) vs M2 (14 Ω, 42, 1.8 × 10⁻³ m², 0.50 T). Ratios M2:M1?
cards.definition: Current sensitivity 1.4; voltage sensitivity 1

cards.term: Electric vs magnetic field lines?
cards.definition: Electric: start on + and end on − (or at infinity). Magnetic: always closed loops

cards.term: Points to ponder: in a frame moving with the charge, the magnetic force vanishes. What explains the motion there?
cards.definition: An electric field appears in that frame — E and B are parts of one electromagnetic field; no preferred frame

cards.term: Is Ampere’s law independent of Biot–Savart?
cards.definition: No: it can be derived from it

cards.term: Chapter 4 formula sheet
cards.definition: Lorentz force: F = q(E + v × B); Force on a wire: F = I l × B; Radius in B: r = mv/qB; Cyclotron frequency: ν = qB/2πm; Loop centre: B = μ₀NI/2R; Long wire: B = μ₀I/2πr; Solenoid: B = μ₀nI; Parallel wires: f = μ₀I₁I₂/2πd; Torque on loop: τ = m × B, m = NIA

cards.definition: A magnetic field can speed up a charge: False (no work); Period of circular motion depends on speed: False; Parallel currents repel: False (attract); Net force on a current loop in uniform B is zero: True; B inside a long solenoid is uniform: True
